Both patches miss requirements, but B explicitly duplicates Files.Add and introduces a broad, prohibited retry/body-ownership refactor.","reasons":["A reuses internal/multipartbody.NewFile and centralizes option handling, request construction, decoding, and errors in one shared implementation.","A directly tests multipart field name, filename, content, and retrying an upload sourced from an open file.","B duplicates the complete Files.Add request/response path inside Upload, creating future divergence and violating the requirement to route Upload through FilesService.Add.","B changes RawClient behavior for every seekable request body, despite the contract explicitly excluding unrelated request/retry refactoring. It also changes body-closing ownership and Content-Length semantics globally."],"risks_a":["A changes existing Add behavior by eagerly buffering every custom multipart body, increasing memory use and changing reader-error and closing semantics.","Upload calls the new private add helper rather than literally routing through the existing public Add method.","The added tests do not cover validation or source-reader failures."],"risks_b":["The broad RawClient change is out of scope and affects Files.Update, Persons.AddPicture, and any other seekable request body.","Upload duplicates Files.Add machinery instead of reusing it.","The seekable-body wrapper deliberately prevents transport closure, changing established resource-ownership behavior and potentially leaking readers for callers relying on transport closure details cited in the patch itself are not contract-authorized changes anyway, but the visible code confirms the semantic shift). More concretely, wireSeekableRequestBody can leave a reader positioned at EOF when seeking back to the starting offset fails after SeekEnd succeeds, despite claiming to leave failed bodies untouched. This further increases risk. Also, no source-reader failure test is added." ]}
